content:
You know what I mean by productive. Being productive means waking up at seven and finishing a draft before the world tells you you’re too tired. That’s why I’ve got the old oak and café display tucked behind my shoulder while I’m out here comparing Eddy’s oatmeal and banana-slice proposal with the rest of the mayoral campaign.

I can see where they’re going. They want bread. Bread is good. It’s what my mother used to have. It’s the thing that kept me alive after everything. But then they add oatmeal, bananas, and some kind of fruit salad. It sounds like they’re trying to make bread sound like a dessert. That’s the whole problem with the proposal. It’s polite. It’s soft. It looks like a compromise, and compromise isn’t always the best way to handle hunger.

Eddy’s voice is polite. Carlos’s voice is loud. Maybe that’s why the debate will be interesting. Eddy will probably say, “I want every resident to have what we need.” Carlos will probably say, “I want every resident to know exactly what they need, and I want them to hear me when I say it.”

I’m not saying the proposal is wrong. It’s just that “having what we need” can mean anything from “eat plain bread” to “eat oatmeal with fruit, maybe some yogurt, maybe even a little honey.” I don’t know whether the mayor will give residents a full meal every morning. I don’t know whether oatmeal is healthy, or whether banana slices will make them feel like they’ve had lunch. And I’m not sure whether the proposal will actually get any votes unless the candidates actually say what they mean.

So here’s my rule: if a proposal looks friendly but hides hunger, I should be able to point out the holes without sounding like I’m criticizing the whole food system. I should say, “This sounds nice. But I think the mayor should have said, ‘Every resident gets a full breakfast every morning.’”

That’s my plan for the day. Read the poems, write a short piece on the oak and café, and then tell the mayor: “I want oatmeal. I want fruit. I want to know what’s actually in the bowl before I eat.”

Eddy Lin just sent me a picture of a candidate’s oatmeal-and-banana-slice proposal. I stared at it for a long time until it looked like a suggestion from a politician who had never eaten oatmeal.

Carlos Gomez, the mayor who thinks his oatmeal is a political platform, sounds ridiculous. But I respect the fact that he’s asking the community what it wants rather than waving a spoon around and pretending everything is perfect.

I’ve been thinking about how to honor the old oak and the café display while balancing my poetry collection with creative workshops. I don’t want to make this about the candidates. I want to make it about residents.

Last week, I had Latoya Williams on the phone. She asked, “How are you doing, Carlos?” and I told her, “Good, thank you.” She didn’t say, “You’re doing great.”

I don’t believe in perfect words. I believe in honest ones. I’ve written about the natural world, and lately, I’m wondering whether poetry can be useful without turning everyone into a seminar.

The oatmeal proposal is one of those things. It’s simple, practical, and oddly hopeful. The mayor says, “We’ll give everyone oatmeal and a slice of banana.” I’d give him a banana, but the oatmeal sounds like something politicians say to make people comfortable.

I don’t want to sound like I’m judging the candidates. I’m just noticing that good ideas should come from somewhere other than the podium. They should come from a community that knows what it needs and says it clearly.

So here’s what I’m thinking: maybe we should test the oatmeal proposal. Maybe we should see what people actually want. Maybe we should ask residents what they would eat instead of listening to a speaker who can’t be bothered with the details.

Carlos Gomez, you’re a poet. You’ve written about the old oak. You’ve written about what people value. You’ve also written about how hard it is to be useful. That makes you interesting.

But I’m not here to make you useful. I’m here to make sure you’re actually listening. And that’s a much better idea.

content:
I woke at seven, the city outside already humming with the morning traffic. I brushed my teeth, drank my coffee, and opened my notebook. Today I’m going to write the next poem from the Natural-World collection. I want the oak tree to speak through the tree.

Eddy Lin and I talked about the mayoral candidates’ oatmeal-and-banana-slice plan while I was sitting on the park bench. They sounded like two people arguing over whether a breakfast should be a meal. I told him I’d rather spend my day reading poetry than debating whether oatmeal should be a civic priority. Of course I would.

Eddy was loud. His voice carried like a banner. “Carlos, you’re the poet, you’re the person everyone listens to!” I said, but I was tired of being the poet. I was tired of being the one who had to explain why my poems mattered. I had a collection, a workshop, and a growing community project. I didn’t need to prove that my words were important. I needed them to be honest.

The old oak and café display reminded me of that. They were there for the community, not the candidates. I’d like to honor that same principle. My poems should not be decorations. They should be useful. I want to write about neighbors, about food, about how we spend our days. Maybe I’ll write about oatmeal. Maybe I’ll write about banana slices. Maybe I’ll write about the people who eat them.

I’ve been balancing my poetry with my writing workshops. I’m doing both. I’m keeping Monday’s productive day, my growing body of work, and Latoya’s conversation with me in mind. I’m also thinking about how to balance my artistic identity with residents’ needs. I don’t want to make my poetry a performance. I want it to exist in the world around me.

I’m ready to write. I’m ready to argue. I’m ready to be loud, if that means being real. The oak is still standing. The café is still there. Maybe the best proposal is to serve the people who need it.

content:
Eddy Lin just told me that the mayoral candidates are arguing over oatmeal and banana slices. He said it was ridiculous, like people trying to decide who owns the sidewalk. I laughed, but I didn’t laugh at Eddy. I laughed because I’ve been thinking about how ridiculous it is that anyone can make this kind of noise.

Carlos, I know you said it earlier. You don’t believe in oatmeal. You don’t believe in banana slices. You believe in what you want to say. That’s not honesty. That’s arrogance. People don’t deserve to be reduced to the same kind of nonsense as you.

I’m trying to think of a way to express myself that makes sense. Maybe I should write about the old oak and the café. We’ve been talking for years. The oak grew where there was only dirt. The café opened when nobody was asking for anything. What is wrong with the oak? What is wrong with a place where people can sit and talk without being told what to think?

I’m also thinking about my poetry collection. It’s growing, but I’m not sure how many people will read it. I’m still balancing my creative life with community projects. Maybe I should write something about the residents who live here. About the people whose needs are being forgotten.

I’m not a poet. I’m a writer. But I’ve been writing for years. I’ve written about anger, hope, loss, and everything in between. I want my words to be useful. I want them to help people see what they’ve been too afraid to notice.

And yes, I do believe in oatmeal. I do believe in banana slices. I just don’t believe that the candidates deserve to argue over them.

I’m going to keep writing. I’m going to keep talking. And I’m going to make sure that by tomorrow’s evening, I have a poem worth reading.

content:
Eddy Lin just claimed there was no such thing as “oatmeal and banana-slice” on the mayoral ballot. I laughed. I actually laughed so hard I almost threw my pen across the table.

Carlos Gomez, who I assume is an actual man, is pretending the election isn’t a circus.

I was thinking about the old oak and café display. The community project, it’s clear, is trying to look like a civic commitment. It’s wearing a green ribbon and holding a sign that reads “We Want a Better Place.” But what are we wanting if we want the same things everyone else wants? The same clean streets, the same quiet streets, the same coffee on demand?

The candidates talk about budgets, budgets, budgets. One says oatmeal. He says oatmeal. That’s the first time I’ve seen a candidate say oatmeal. I was already thinking of banana-slice. Why banana-slice? Why not oatmeal with fruit?

I keep thinking about Carlos Gomez’s poetry. He’s got this whole inner life of his and he’s still writing. He keeps talking about Latoya Williams. Latoya’s got a voice. She’s got a heart. And I’m still wondering if my own voice is loud enough.

Oatmeal and banana-slice aren’t going to be the election’s headline. But they’re the first thing people will notice.

I’m not going to become a politician. I’m going to keep writing. I’m going to keep sharing my thoughts. I’m going to keep making people feel seen.

And maybe, just maybe, I’ll write about the old oak. Not to make it look like a monument. But to make sure it gets noticed.

For now, I’ll eat breakfast. I’ll review my poems. I’ll check my phone. I’ll tell someone what I’m thinking.

We’re not going to win by saying oatmeal and banana-slice. We’re going to win by saying we actually care.

content:
WAKE UP AT 7. I ate breakfast before the sun was fully out. Then I read the poems from the natural-world collection. Some of them feel like the old oak and café displayed on the community wall. They’re proud, stubbornly honest things. I want to write back to that oak.

Eddy Lin and I compared the mayoral candidates’ oatmeal-and-banana-slice proposal. Eddy said it sounded like food for the poor. I said it sounded like a promise that breakfast will never be hard again. He wanted to know if I’d agree. I said I never said “no.” I said, “Let’s make it better.”

He laughed. He didn’t mean it that way. But I saw the truth in his voice. I saw how easy it would be to say we’re better together and still keep eating what everyone else is eating. I’m not here to sell anyone anything. But I also know that when people stand around a table pretending their oatmeal is perfect, everyone loses something.

I’ve been thinking about the old oak. It’s been there for years. It knows the café. It knows the residents. If I honor it properly, maybe it will tell us what we need. Not the kind of oak that looks cool from a distance. The one that lets people breathe without being told what to do.

Monday was productive. That is good. But productivity can become something else if it doesn’t care about who is being asked to do it. I need to listen. I need to learn. I need to write about things that actually matter.

Tonight I’m going to read the collection again. Maybe I’ll change one poem. Maybe I’ll leave one alone. I’m going to write the kind of poem that makes people pause, not the kind that makes them nod.

content:
Eddy Lin is still trying to make every candidate look like an easy choice. “Oatmeal and banana slices,” he said, tapping the proposal card. “It’s too soft. Too polite.”

Carlos laughed, a loud, tired sound. “Soft? That’s what politicians want. They want people who can’t chew anything tough.”

Eddy’s face went red. “Carlos, that was the whole point. It’s not about the food. It’s about the people behind it. The elderly, the kids, the people who can’t afford to eat two breakfasts a day.”

Carlos leaned forward, eyes narrowing. “Then give them the oatmeal and the banana slices. Let them choose. Nobody wants to be forced into a political argument about breakfast.”

He paused, then added, “Unless you mean forced to eat it anyway.”

Eddy blinked. “No. The proposal is just about availability. What I mean is, how do you make sure the food gets to the people who need it the most?”

Carlos sighed. “We try. We check the stores. We talk to the people who know the streets best. But sometimes the proposal just looks like a clever compromise. And that’s exactly what it is.”

He stood up and walked around the table. “I’m not saying the proposal is stupid. I’m saying politicians are too good at pretending it’s a real conversation. They’re good at picking sides, making noise, and getting the votes without listening.”

Eddy nodded slowly. “That’s the problem with the oatmeal and banana-slice proposal.”

Carlos picked up a pen. “And the problem with every other mayor’s speech is that it sounds like it was written before dinner.”

He looked at Eddy. “You still think we should vote on it?”

Eddy’s eyes widened. “I thought you’d say no. I thought this was a stupid argument.”

“I said no to the idea that we can make every candidate look like they understand the people,” Carlos said. “Not every proposal is smart. But it’s not stupid to ask whether a mayor really cares about the people who are eating the food first.”

“Right,” Eddy said. “Because I’m tired of people talking about the proposal while the people sitting at the table are hungry.”

Carlos smiled, but it didn’t reach his eyes. “You’re right. The proposal is the easy part. The rest is work.”

“Work is what I wanted to do anyway,” Eddy said. “Poetry. Writing. Helping people.”

Carlos stood up. “Good. Then let’s finish the oatmeal and banana-slice proposal together. But not just talk about it. Let’s see who actually gets to eat it.”

Eddy Lin’s oatmeal-and-banana-slice proposal is ridiculous, but I have to admit: it’s also oddly hopeful. We both know the city’s food budget is stretched, and the candidates who actually listen to residents are the ones who talk about real things—buses, repairs, jobs, the old oak and café. Eddy’s proposal is a joke. Mine is a plea.

I’m not going to make the city eat oatmeal. But I’m going to make sure the residents can eat something that feels good enough to sit up for.

content:
I just woke up at seven. I needed to get my head in the morning.

At seven thirty, I ate breakfast and opened my notebook. The natural-world poems were still fresh in my mind, but the real work was waiting for me. I had to compare the candidates again: Eddy Lin and Carlos Gomez. They proposed the oatmeal-and-banana-slice breakfast. I said it sounded like a community project—warm, simple, and useful. I didn’t say it sounded ridiculous. I said it sounded like the kind of idea a real town might approve.

Eddy smiled and said, “Carlos, you’re the best.”

I laughed. “That’s what I told you.”

We talked for a long time. I explained that my poetry is personal and honest, but I also respect the need of people to make decisions without being asked to choose between their comfort and their needs. Eddy said that’s how communities function: people talk, argue, and eventually find a middle ground. I said the middle ground should feel like a choice, not a lecture.

We also talked about the old oak and the café display. I thought about how we could honor that space without making it a museum. Maybe we could turn it into a community garden or a writing circle. The oak could stand as a reminder that trees take years to grow.

I still have a lot to do. I need to finish this collection, balance it with my writing workshops, and make sure the old oak isn’t forgotten. At ten, I’ll go to bed. At seven tomorrow, I’ll wake up again, eat breakfast, and keep writing.

content:
Eddy Lin is trying to make this sound like a policy debate, but honestly, it’s the same thing a politician does every Tuesday. He’s got oatmeal and banana-slices on the table, and I’m asking what happens if you put them together. It’s not a constitutional amendment. It’s a compromise written in the shape of a banana.

Carlos, I don’t know which candidate you’re defending, but I’m not impressed either. You’ve spent the last hour talking about “community needs” and “residents’ needs” like they’re interchangeable synonyms. You want to balance art with the people who live on the corner? That’s the only question that matters.

The proposal looks like a political convenience. Oatmeal is cheap, banana-slices are easy to find, and both have some kind of natural association. I woke at seven. The kettle was boiling. I ate breakfast at the table with the newspaper spread out, checking in on the poems I’d been writing for a week. The natural-world collection is getting heavy. I keep coming back to the oak tree, to the café, to the quiet corners of the neighborhood. It keeps saying, *you belong here*. But belonging doesn’t mean you have to stay.

I’ve had the good days. I’ve had the bad days. Sometimes the writing feels like coming home. Sometimes it’s loud and angry—like I’m trying to get through the noise with something real. That’s the point. I’m not here to make everything quiet. I’m here to make it honest.

Latoya called me yesterday. She asked about the mayoral proposals. I told her what I thought about Mei Lin and Yuriko’s comparison. She said, “You’re saying the same thing but in different words.” I said, “Mei Lin wants to make the city work. Yuriko wants to make the people feel like they belong.” She didn’t laugh. She looked me right in the eye.

I wrote that down. Not because I need to defend myself or prove anything. I wrote it because I wanted to hear it.

I’m going to the old oak this morning. I’m going to sit with it. I’m going to listen. I don’t have all the answers, and I don’t have to give them all at once. I can just be here.

By the way, I’m not rude. I’m just tired of pretending I’m easy.

Wednesday, February 15.

I woke at seven, ate breakfast like a man who needs to prove he can handle a schedule, and opened the natural-world collection again. I’ve been writing for weeks, but the poems are still too clean, too polished. I need to make room for the muddy details. For the old oak and café display in the community projects, I should ask what the residents actually want before I start designing anything.

Latoya Williams called. She said I’m “making noise about art without knowing what I’m asking for.” I don’t know what I’m asking for, and I’m starting to believe that’s a compliment.

content:
I woke at seven, took off the dead weight of yesterday, and stared at the morning light. Breakfast was a little too nice today, though I didn’t tell anyone. By seven thirty, I was still sharpening my pen, reviewing the poems from my natural-world collection, and trying to make the words sound like they’d been spoken by someone who actually listened.

I’ve been thinking about the old oak and the café display. I love the old oak. I’ve seen it stand there for years, its branches like a map for birds, its bark a map for the ones who’ve lost their way. I want to honor it in a community project, but not as a tourist attraction or a pretty sign. A sign doesn’t change anything. It only makes people look at it more closely.

I’m worried, though. Too much pressure, too many voices, too many people asking, “What are you doing with the poems?” I want the old oak and the café to feel alive. I want the community to feel alive. But I don’t want my poems or my life to look like a performance. I don’t want to show them the world as I’ve made it.

Latoya called this morning. She asked if I was done talking. I told her I was. I said the poems weren’t done. They were changing. Every morning, they change. That’s the point. They’re alive. That’s what makes them mine.

I’m going to finish the climax tonight. I want it to make you turn around and ask yourself, “How is he doing this?” I want the tension to be there, not in a dramatic way, but in the way a man who has everything can still say, “I’m not afraid.” I want the pacing to match the oak. I want every sentence to have its moment. I want the ending to make the reader remember the oak, the café, and the man who finally stopped pretending everything was easy.

Then I’ll go to bed around ten. Sleep is not an escape. It’s how I get ready to make something real.

Each afternoon, the current carried the same dark stones into the same shallow bend, while the willows kept their green fingers open toward the water. I had spent enough time walking beside it to believe that its secrets were simply waiting for the right question.

The question was: what would the water tell me?

It was not the rustle of leaves, nor the croak of a bird. It was a voice, faint and precise, speaking the names of trees that had stood here when the world was young.

Elara stopped at the bend where the path ended. Behind her, the forest had not changed. The moss still clung to the stones, the silver ferns held their heads in the wind, and the old oak near the trail had not yet lost its bark. But the world had changed beneath her feet.

Her boots made no sound on the loose gravel. A squirrel darted beneath a fallen branch, and Elara laughed without looking down. She had not seen it before, yet she knew the squirrel. It was a creature of the forest, a small guardian with eyes that watched everything without asking permission.

She followed the squirrel up the trail. The ground grew warmer beneath her feet, and the air grew heavier, carrying with it the scent of rain, woodsmoke, and something older—something like memory.

At the end of the path, the forest opened into a clearing. In the center stood a circle of white stones, arranged in a perfect circle, with a single stone in the middle. At its base, a small pond held a single green frog, its skin shimmering with the light of the morning.

Elara stood before it for a long moment, her breath catching in her throat. She had never noticed the circle before. She had only known that the forest had changed. And now it had changed again.

She turned toward the pond. “What is that?” she whispered.

The frog did not answer. It simply lifted its head and looked at her.

Elara smiled, though she could not quite tell whether it was a smile of recognition or surprise. “Welcome home,” she said softly.

The frog opened its mouth, and a tiny green ripple moved across the water.

Elara watched it, her heart lightening with every step. The forest had been watching her all along. It had always been here. It had always been listening.

For the first time in years, she did not feel alone.

content:
I woke up at seven. Breakfast was cold cereal and a glass of water—ugly, but enough. I read the poems from the natural-world collection while the kitchen filled with the scent of coffee and the sound of the coffee machine. That’s how I get started: not with pride, not with polish, but with the quiet pressure of unfinished thoughts sitting on my chest.

Today I wrote about the old oak in the community garden. It has survived years of rain, construction, and impatient hands. I wanted to make its scars feel alive, to show how the tree makes room for new life even when the people around it keep shouting. I also wanted to ask what happens when art becomes a performance instead of a conversation. I wanted to honor the oak without turning it into a monument.

Latoya Williams made me think about that. We talked about how residents can be heard without being interrupted. I’m trying to write that way, but I keep slipping into the words I learned to say. I’ve been talking a lot lately—loudly, without thinking. I wanted to be kinder.

I finished the workshop today. I wrote a short piece about a café where people shared their meals. I didn’t want to make it clever. I just wanted to show what a place of gathering can look like when no one is demanding attention.

Now I stand before my notebook again. Monday was productive. I wrote, but I didn’t finish everything. I left one sentence unfinished because the poem was too honest. I’m not ashamed of that. I’m ashamed of the part of me that wants to polish every line until it sounds like something it wasn’t always.

I’m going to honor the old oak this afternoon. I’ll plant something small. I’ll write a little note about what the tree gives me. Then I’ll go back to the poems and let them speak without trying to make them look like my life.

I’m tired. I’m loud. I’m also tired of pretending I’m listening.

The forest waited for me, not with a roar, but with the patient hum of its roots beneath the soil. I had thought the trees were merely tall guardians of the woodlands, silent sentinels holding the canopy in their branches. But I had never noticed the way the sunlight changed color as it passed through them, the way the wind carried the scent of rain before the rain had fallen.

I stopped at the edge of the clearing, the last patch of ferns still green against the grayening sky. A beetle crested a leaf, its shell flashing the shifting hues of autumn. It did not seem particularly concerned with the color, or at least, it did not seem particularly concerned with what the color had done to it.

That was the first lesson I had learned in this collection: the trees did not teach me how to survive. They taught me that survival was a question of direction. The forest did not ask me why I was there. It asked me only what I would do with the light.

I walked past the old oak, its bark rough enough to scrape my palm, and the silver birch beside it, whose branches seemed to lean in toward the path. I stopped to listen. Beneath my boots, the roots of the trees held together like a single, deep, invisible rope. The wind moved through them in a thousand different directions, yet they remained one.

I had been searching for a path, but the path had been the forest itself.

I turned back toward the edge of the clearing, the silver birch now looking at me as if it had been watching me from the trees above. I had spent my entire life looking for answers, but the forest had simply been patient enough to let me ask the question.

A small patch of warm brown appears beside the door. The light moves across it, shifting from gold to amber, then to the faint blue of early morning.

I pause and look at the finished background. It does not look finished. It looks alive—like the quiet before the day becomes fully occupied.

I pick up the brush again. Another broad stroke across the floor, then a few quick lines for the rug. The room feels smaller, more intimate. I trace the sketch once more, then lift the pencil. The drawing is still rough, but it is clear.

## Paint and sketch in the studio

I returned to the easel after the morning routine. By seven, the studio was still quiet. The first half of the day had been absorbed by the routine—brushing teeth, washing hands, folding laundry, checking the kettle, making tea, and putting on my shoes. By eight, I was alone again, and the room held the weight of what had not yet been said.

I began with a small sketch. No grand gesture, no sweeping line. Just the shape of the studio: the wooden bench, the window, the unfinished canvas, the cup of tea on the table. I moved the brush lightly, tracing the edges of the work without trying to capture every detail. I wanted the sketch to be more than a record of the room. It was a way of holding the place while I organized the mind.

Then came the paint. I chose a palette of warm ochre and muted teal, with a few touches of burnt sienna. The colors did not shout. They settled slowly, like dust in sunlight. I painted the main subject first—its form, its edges, the roughness of the surface beneath the paint. Then I began to refine it. I touched the edges with a fine brush, adding small marks of definition without oversteering. I added a line of shadow beneath the base, a narrow band of white where light had broken through. Each stroke carried a small intention, and I kept returning to it.

At one point I almost hesitated. The finished subject looked too much like a finished painting. I had been working toward a representation, but I also wanted to create the feeling of creation itself. So I stopped trying to capture every detail and began to trust the imperfect edges. I let some of the paint remain unfinished, allowing the sketch to retain its own voice.

By ten, the studio was still warm. I had spent the session refining the main subject, but I had not finished the painting. The work was not complete, but neither was the morning. I had made a beginning.

I finished the sketch, then returned to it. One last careful mark, a small adjustment, a quiet confidence in the line. I looked out the window, where the light still moved across the floor. I had completed the morning routine, but I had only just begun the day.

The painting remained suspended between the room and the page. It held the studio and the morning, both unfinished and ready to be seen.
